chooseN.prompt: Pick any 4 of these 5 questions to answer.

tiers.label: Recycle
tiers.sublabel: what you cannot refuse, reduce, or reuse

scenes.prompt: Choose the waste management strategy that is matched with the correct example.

options.text: Refuse: Choose products that use less packaging

tableRow.label: Refuse
tableRow.value: Choose products that use less packaging

options.misconception: This example is really about Reduce, not Refuse - choosing less packaging cuts down what you consume, it doesn't turn down something you never needed in the first place.

options.text: Reduce: Give unwanted toys and books to hospitals or schools

tableRow.label: Reduce
tableRow.value: Give unwanted toys and books to hospitals or schools

options.misconception: This example is really about Reuse - giving an item a second life with a new owner keeps it in use, it doesn't lower how much you consume.

options.text: Reuse: Not using single-use plastic
options.misconception: This example is really about Refuse - declining single-use plastic at the point of purchase means never taking it on in the first place, not reusing something you already have.

options.text: Repurpose: Making a flower pot from a used plastic bottle

tableRow.label: Repurpose
tableRow.value: Making a flower pot from a used plastic bottle

options.correctRationale: This is the one pair that actually matches: turning a used bottle into a flower pot gives a discarded object a new function, which is exactly what repurposing means - the same trick households use with jars-as-pen-holders or tyres-as-planters.

scenes.prompt: Recycling of paper is a good practice, but recycled paper should not be used as food packaging because

options.text: recycled paper may release colour/dyes onto food items
options.correctRationale: Recycled paper carries ink and dye residue from its previous life, which can leach into food - the same reason greasy, ink-stained pizza boxes are rejected from paper recycling instead of being turned back into food packaging.

options.text: recycled paper is not absorbent
options.misconception: Recycling doesn't strip paper of its absorbency - the real food-safety concern is chemical and dye contamination carried over from the paper's earlier use, not its texture.

options.text: recycled paper can cause infection due to release of methane
options.misconception: Methane is released by decomposing organic waste in landfills, not by recycled paper - this option mixes up two unrelated waste-management facts.

options.text: recycled paper is costly
options.misconception: Cost is the opposite problem - recycled paper is generally cheaper than virgin paper. Cost has nothing to do with why it's unsafe for direct food contact.

scenes.prompt: According to the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016, waste should be segregated into three categories. Which row correctly sorts waste into Wet, Dry, and Hazardous?

options.text: Wet: cooked food & vegetable peels | Dry: used bulbs, fluorescent lamps | Hazardous: plastic carry bags, bottles, newspaper, cardboard
options.misconception: Dry and hazardous are swapped here - bulbs and fluorescent lamps contain mercury and belong in hazardous waste, while plastic bags, bottles, newspaper, and cardboard are ordinary dry waste.

options.text: Wet: coffee & tea powder, garden waste | Dry: plastic carry bags, bottles, newspaper, cardboard | Hazardous: expired medicines, razors, paint cans
options.correctRationale: This matches how municipal segregation actually works: green/wet bins for biodegradable kitchen and garden waste, blue/dry bins for recyclable plastics and paper, and red/hazardous bins for anything that can injure or poison - sharps, expired medicine, and paint.

options.text: Wet: leftover food & vegetable peels | Dry: coffee & tea powder, garden waste | Hazardous: insect repellents, cleaning solutions
options.misconception: Coffee and tea powder and garden waste are wet/biodegradable waste, not dry waste - they were placed in the wrong column here.

options.text: Wet: uncooked food, tea leaves | Dry: old crockery, frying pans | Hazardous: coffee & tea powder, garden waste
options.misconception: Coffee, tea powder, and garden waste are biodegradable wet waste, not hazardous - and old crockery/frying pans are general dry waste, not a hazard category.

scenes.prompt: Effective segregation of waste at the point of generation is very important. Select the statements that correctly explain why: i) less waste goes to landfills, ii) it is better for public health and the environment, iii) it helps in reducing the waste generated, iv) it results in deterioration of a waste picker's health.

options.text: both i) and ii)
options.correctRationale: Segregated waste sends less to landfills (because recyclables and compostables are diverted) and reduces contamination and disease spread - both genuine, well-documented benefits of source segregation.

options.text: both i) and iii)
options.misconception: Statement iii) confuses segregation with reduction. Segregating waste sorts it into streams for proper processing - it doesn't shrink the amount of waste generated in the first place; that's what the 'Reduce' R does.

options.text: both ii) and iii)
options.misconception: Same mix-up as above: iii) describes reduction, not segregation. Segregation and reduction are two different Rs in the waste hierarchy.

options.text: both i) and iv)
options.misconception: Statement iv) reverses the real effect. Keeping hazardous and wet waste separated from dry recyclables actually protects waste pickers by reducing their exposure to sharp, toxic, or contaminated material - it improves their safety, not deteriorates it.

scenes.prompt: When recycling a plastic water bottle with a cap, what should you do with the cap?

options.text: Throw the cap in the garbage can and put the bottle in the recycling bin
options.misconception: Separating them sends a perfectly recyclable cap to landfill for no reason - caps are recyclable too, they just need to stay attached to make it through sorting.

options.text: Screw the cap back onto the bottle, then put both in the recycling bin
options.correctRationale: Bottle caps are usually a different plastic (HDPE/PP) than the bottle body (PET) and are too small for sorting machinery to catch on their own - screwing the cap back on keeps it attached through the sorting process so both get recycled instead of the cap falling through as litter.

options.text: Screw the cap back onto the bottle, then put both in the garbage can
options.misconception: This throws away a fully recyclable bottle and cap together - keeping them attached is right, but they belong in the recycling bin, not the garbage.

options.text: Recycle the cap separately from the bottle
options.misconception: Small caps dropped loose onto a sorting line usually fall through the machinery's screens and end up as landfill or litter instead of being recycled - keeping the cap on the bottle is what actually gets it recycled.

scenes.title: Recap: The 5 Rs
recapLines: Recycle what you can't refuse, reduce, or reuse
